utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have asked on the end of the testimony, indeed after Mr. Naumovski put some questions, whether I could add only one question which was omitted because we changed the way we were progressing, and you told me that I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is literally only one question which I omitted from the summary. It is point 71 in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Kovacic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ceko, I omitted -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I omitted to put a question to you as we were going through the summary of your statement. Please tell the Court, to the best of your recollection, who was in charge of artillery in the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the brigade headquarters it was Blazenko Ramljak who was chief of artillery and in charge of artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other specialised unit or group that would go beyond the field of artillery, for example, like rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Marko Lujic was, nicknamed Markesa?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever -- was he ever, at any point in time, chief of artillery or anything similar to that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Marko Lujic, nicknamed Markesa, was never a member of the command, let alone chief of artillery in the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm here also referring to the document D82/2, where a list of members of brigade command exist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nice Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, tell us, please, why the Muslims of Vitez were arrested and detained.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims from Vitez at the beginning of the conflict -- that is to say, from the 16th of April, 1993 -- were most probably interned for several reasons. I think that one of the reasons was their very own safety. On that day when the conflict broke out, since there were several men, several units in Vitez, and then also there were lots of refugees who were in Vitez and whose housing problems had not been resolved. So that was for their own safety. And secondly, for the safety of the HVO soldiers, because you could not distinguish amongst the civilians who were real civilians and who were members of the BH army. I imagine that those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you imagine those were the reasons, Major. I'm going to ask -- I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could have D88/2, the map produced by the Defence. Perhaps that could be laid on the ELMO. I'm so sorry not to have given you notice. I thought I had my own, but apparently it's being reproduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at this map on the ELMO, Major. So that we can have an idea of the scale of the town that you're talking about, the squares on this map are kilometre squares, I think, and so the totality of the centre of Vitez fits well within one square kilometre, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please could you repeat your question and clarify it? I didn't manage to register everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The blue square marks on the map are kilometre squares. They make it quite clear that Vitez is a town sufficiently small -- if you just look at the scale of the map, Major. You've been in the army -- but Vitez basically fits in, fits well within, one kilometre square; it's a very small town. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you're telling us you imagine something happened and that something was the detention of all the Muslims or nearly all the Muslims of your town, you must know why they were detained. It's not a question of guessing. Are you saying that they were detained for their own safety, or were they detained as part of a planned persecution and in order to gain control of the town? Which was it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. There was never any planned persecution or mistreatment or anything vis-à-vis the Muslims. Simply a conflict broke out. And in the town of Vitez, in the centre of town -- you said yourself it's a small town -- there were lots of people. There was chaos. And I know a lot of people who reported themselves, who reported at the adult education centre. They came in and they asked to stay there for their own personal safety reasons. I know that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, you also know that the Viteska Brigade was engaged in rounding up and detaining Muslims. Why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. The Viteska Brigade was never engaged in rounding up Muslims. That was never its task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that they took no part in detaining any Muslim? We've had quite a lot of evidence in this case. I'm not going to weary you with the detail of it. But are you really telling us that no member of the Viteska Brigade had anything to do with arresting any Muslim?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single member of the Viteska Brigade had nothing to do [as interpreted] with arresting Muslims, and I mentioned that it was done by the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Karlo Grabovac? Do you count him as a member of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karlo Grabovac was a member of the brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there's been evidence that he rounded up and helped in the detention of Muslims, how could that be? Was he on loan to the police?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Karlo Grabovac never worked for the police. First of all, I'm not aware of that, that Karlo Grabovac took part in such actions. He lives in Rijeka, and the battalion that is within the Viteska Brigade had its headquarters in Rijeka, Sumarija. And since at that time the expected attack was to come from Vranjska and Kruscica and from the direction of Rijeka, he was there with the intention of stopping passage further to town. And I really am not aware of his having participated in any of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to take you through the evidence that there is. It would take too long. But tell me this: Are you now saying that the Viteska Brigade had absolutely nothing to do with the detention of prisoners at all?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I claim that Viteska Brigade had nothing to do with the detention of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness see 591.1, please, which is probably in the form of the affidavit of Colonel Morsink. 591.1, I think it is. It's just the list. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll be good enough to look at this, which will be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just that we are sure about the way that the document -- this document was excluded when it was used by -- during the testimony of Mr. Morsink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The list of the prisoners, it was excluded, and then Mr. Morsink swore or introduced a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to be sure that this is the one which was enclosed to affidavit statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think the position is that it wasn't excluded. It was not technically admitted because it wasn't dealt with. And it was then dealt with by affidavit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at this document, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it could be laid on the ELMO. The front page is fine and the top part of it most helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document which comes from the Viteska Brigade. And I'm afraid that the title has not been translated, but nothing else needs to be, it being just a list. But tell us that title. Just read it out, please, the three words, if you can. Or if you can't read the three words, read the second word, beginning with "Privedenih." Read those words for us, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here that it says underneath the letterhead "list of persons brought into custody."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the handwriting is from the major -- I beg your pardon -- from the monitor, now a lieutenant colonel in the Dutch service, to whom this list was provided, and we then see 300 names on the list. Can you explain, please, how the Viteska Brigade, if it was not involved in detention of Muslims, was listing people like this.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you exactly, I see here in the letterhead it says Viteska Brigade, and I see that it concerns a list of detained persons but I don't see that it was done by the Viteska Brigade at least I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know "done," do you mean the list wasn't done or the detention wasn't done?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it's anyone from the Viteska Brigade that compiled this list. It doesn't say who drew up the list. There is no signature, no name, no nothing. I can't say anything because whoever does something is supposed to sign it to show that he stands by it. It is a fact that people were detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was provided, on the evidence, by Borislav Jozic. I think you tell us he is a man that we can trust; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what would Borislav Jozic be doing with a list like this handing it over to a monitor at the time, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what Borislav Jozic did with this list and who he gave it to if he made it. I know that he worked on security affairs with us, but I'm not sure that he did this. Even if he did do this, this is just an assumption, he probably did it so that these people would be recorded and that something could be done with these people so that they could be released. I don't know what else could have been the case. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my last question on the list derives from the evidence of Colonel Morsink, and it's in light of your last answer where you suggest that these people were listed for their own benefit. Can you give any explanation for why, if the Viteska Brigade were listing people on that basis, they should exclude the children and the women who were there who made the total number detained much larger than 300 as Colonel Morsink's evidence would suggest? Why would the children be omitted, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say that I was sure that this was made by someone from the Viteska Brigade, Borislav Jozic included. However, I did say that I think that if Borislav Jozic did it, he did it for the reasons I mentioned. I never said that women and children were detained there. That was never the case, because I personally passed there quite often. There were no women or children detained there at the time. It was only military age able-bodied men who were detained at the cinema at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how many military police were there who, between them, were capable of controlling all these different detention facilities, please, Major? How many?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the military police, they were in the building where the command was. There were 16 or 17 or 18 people. This was at the adult education centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard of a lot of detention facilities in Vitez. You've listed them yourself. Can you tell us, please, overall in Vitez, how many military police were there who, on your evidence, were capable of both detaining -- sorry, arresting and detaining all these 300 or it may be 500 people. How many?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many were needed for interning all of them in these places that were mentioned, but I know how many people from the military police were in the building where the command was where most of the Muslims were interned or detained. As I mentioned, the SDK premises and the chess club premises, that is where the policemen probably had shifts of two or three men, but I didn't pass there very often, I passed there maybe once or twice. But this, the cinema, the adult education centre, I passed there every day because that's where the command post was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you going to give me a figure please for the number of military police available to conduct this entire arrest and detention operation or not?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I won't, because I don't know this and I have nothing to do with this organisation of the detention of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, you know perfectly well that the Viteska Brigade was involved in the apprehension and detention of prisoners and it was involved in it in full, and that you've got to come here and give evidence that you know to be false. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true at all. I don't know of the Viteska Brigade having participated and that is a matter of fact. I assert it did not take part in it at all, and I was not brought here to provide false testimony. I came here to help reach the truth and I'm just telling the truth and nothing else and I know -- and I say what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I turn to Ahmici which is my next topic, just help me with this, Major. Did you find the developments within your very small town between the spring of 1992 and the summer of 1993, did you find those developments a bit uncomfortable and by that I mean, did you see the developing oppression or persecution of Muslims something that was, frankly, a bit uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long question. I'll try to answer all of it. As far as I can remember, you mentioned the period from the summer of 1992 to the summer of 1993. The situation was not like that at all. At the time, together with the Muslims, with the BH army, we defended the defence lines. We were defending ourselves from the Serb aggression, from the JNA, and from the army of Republika Srpska; Jajce, Turbe, Novi Travnik et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that when we look at that period in a little more detail. You told us last week that, when you were trying to tell us what was in Cerkez's mind, I think that you agreed with him in principle, something like that. Was there any attitude of Cerkez about events that you disagreed with?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just explain in which period what I had in mind? Could you please just clarify this a bit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to you tell us over the whole period of time. Did you find yourself at any period of time between April 1992, even the end of 1991 and the summer of 1993, did you find yourself ever disagreeing with what appeared to be Cerkez's view of things?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with him. I agreed with his positions, but we didn't talk very much. We talked, for the most, part in 1991 at the time when there was an open aggression against the Republic of Croatia. We saw what this was all about and what could come out of this, and that is when we discussed these matters. However, later, from 1992 onwards when the headquarters were established, we did not discuss this. Our priority was defence from the Serb aggression at that time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we come to the events of Ahmici itself, and don't hesitate to tell us what you knew was in Cerkez's mind, because that's what we want to know about. But before we come to that, you, of course, spent a lot of time in your depot or your office, didn't you, on the day of the 16th so you can't really tell us very much about what actually happened from firsthand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have put a question that is a bit complicated, and I can't really answer it. You're putting words into my mouth that I knew what Mario Cerkez wanted. I didn't quite understand the question. I don't know what Mario Cerkez wanted at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My mistake entirely. I'll break it up into two parts. First of all, because you were in your office or in your depot most of the day, you don't have any firsthand knowledge of what actually happened at Ahmici, do you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, no information about what happened during those first days in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are unable --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I did not have any information during those first days, from the 16th onwards, about what had happened in Ahmici. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't say, in fact, one way or another, whether Cerkez was involved in the massacre at Ahmici or not, can you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say, and I assert with certainty that Cerkez did not take part in any massacre, let alone the massacre in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you assert that, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that on the basis of the fact that I know where Cerkez was until the morning, and I know that there was an attack of the BH army against the Croat positions, and I know that he was engaged in the directions that we mentioned: Kruscica, Vranjska, headquarters. I heard nothing else. He worked on these jobs and he was probably around Kruscica, around Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see that brings me to the second part of my --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is what our unit was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That brings me to the second part of my first question. The answers that you've just given are all based on things that you were told; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the question has not been put to me very precisely. What kind of things are you referring to that were told to me? I cannot see from your question what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Major, when you say that he was in Kruscica or matters of that sort, that's because you were told things, because you had information from other people, and that's what you base your answer to this Chamber on.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear that. I know in the morning on the 16th of April 1993, in the morning at 5.00, I saw his car in front of the house. Since we live next door to one another, there's a 30-metre distance at the maximum and that morning I did not see him but I saw his car in front of the house, and I saw him at brigade headquarters and 6.00. I don't know the exact time but I think it was around that time, and I know he was nowhere else because we had our men from the Viteska Brigade, from that unit. They were stationed in the Sumarija building at Rijeka, and their only assignment was to try to blockade the roads from Kruscica and Vranjska via Rijeka towards the centre of town. Mario was probably in that area, because he did not have members of his own military anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I'm addressing myself to the witness, in the interest of interpretation, you must slow down because we are having a great deal of difficulty in following you. So you will be followed much better if you slow down because the interpreters are trying to keep pace with you and I don't know whether we really are able to follow. So please slow down.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll try to speak slower. Should I repeat what I've been saying so far? Your Honours, do I need to repeat what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major I will attempt to help you get the rhythm of speech and it's more convenient for the Court by slowing down myself. You make take the rhythm from me. Your last answer might appear to be contradictory. You are saying that Cerkez was most likely in the area where they were trying to blockade the roads from Kruscica and Vranjska, and earlier in the same answer, you said he was definitely at home because that's where his car was. Can you resolve that apparent conflict for me?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can and I think that there's no contradiction whatsoever. I'm talking about the 16th of April, 1993 about 5.00 in the morning when I saw the car in front of his house. Then I said that I saw him again in the brigade headquarters about 6.00, I think it was about 6.00 in the morning. And I also said that I assume he was where our unit was and the task of our unit was to block the roads from Kruscica and Vranjska leading towards the centre of town. So I see no contradiction there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will just come back to that little detail in just a minute, but I want your help with this: You actually weren't with Cerkez. You worked with the active part of your brigade who was, on your account, elsewhere. Can you tell us, please, who, apart of course from Cerkez himself, is the person who can most easily help us with what the Viteska Brigade was doing that night? Who was on active duty with the Viteska Brigade and who can come to this Court and tell us the truth? Name someone, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you said that I was not with the active part of the brigade and then later that I was with the active part of the brigade. That is not correct. I was not with the active part of the brigade. I was in the warehouse, the command post of the brigade, and the headquarters of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia on that day, the 16th of April. Your second question that I name somebody who might know more as to where Cerkez was that day, probably the other members of the command such as Zeljko Sajevic, Ivo Sucic, Mario Rajic, who were operative officers -- sorry, Mario Rajic was not there, I think, the first two days as far as I can remember, so Zeljko Sajevic and Ivo Sucic, they may know where Mario was at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zeljko Sajevic -- well, the first name you mentioned -- what was he doing on that night, then, on your understanding?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Sajevic -- I'm sorry. I may have made a mistake. That night he was ill; he had a cold. And he was in the headquarters and I know that the commander, Mario Cerkez, allowed him to go home. Then I know he was there in the morning again, because I went there. Zeljko Sajevic was there. And then later on -- I don't remember too well -- I think he was released to go home again in the morning. So I'm not quite sure. I can't remember the details. But I know he was ill. He had a very bad cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a minute. In your long answer about who was available to help, you actually name Zeljko Sajevic twice. Now, we've had evidence from him that he was unwell. He had a piece of paper to show that he was unwell. Do you remember giving your first answer to the Judges and you named Zeljko Sajevic? How had you forgotten this little detail? Or is it possible that Zeljko Sajevic wasn't ill? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible that he was not ill, because I remember that he was ill. And second of all, it was seven years ago. I never thought about these things. And it is difficult to recall names at a given moment. But I remembered his name since he was the first operative officer. He was chief of staff. And so at first I thought he may be the most qualified person. I just forgot that that morning he had this cold. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that I've got this correct, you've actually remembered back over seven years a man saying he had a cold, have you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that the man said. I remembered because I saw him myself. He is a delicate person and he gets colds easily and often has one. So I saw it. I didn't hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other two men who you say could give us firsthand accounts, Sucic and Rajic, where do they live now, if they're still alive?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are both alive. Mario Rajic is living in Kruscica. I mentioned him. But it seems to me that he was not in the brigade headquarters the first couple of days. I remembered that later. As for Ivo Sucic, I'm not sure where he is residing now. I know he's not in Vitez. He's abroad or somewhere. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as we try to find out who it is can help us with firsthand knowledge of what the Viteska Brigade was doing that night, are we down to Sucic now, or is there anybody else you can think of who might be able to come and help?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I thought these would be the most qualified persons who should know most. Now let me think who else. In the command at the time, Blazenko Ramljak was chief of artillery, Jozo Zuljevic, Borislav Jozic. I think he might be the most qualified. Unfortunately, the man was killed. So I'm afraid I can't remember any others. But if necessary, I can try and think a little longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you think of another name in the course of evidence of somebody who can come and give an account, do so. Major, as I understand your evidence -- correct me if I'm wrong -- the behaviour of the Viteska Brigade that night was wholly proper and wholly lawful. Is that what you're telling us? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that when we identify someone who could come and help the Chamber, there could be no reason arising from the conduct on that night known to you that would deter anyone from coming here to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fear I haven't understood your question. I understood you to be asking me whether these people that I have named, if they were to come here to testify before Their Honours, that they knew what the brigade was doing at that time. Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to abandon the question and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, Major Ceko, let me see that I have your evidence correctly about the morning of the 16th and Mr. Cerkez's whereabouts. Your evidence is that at 5.00, when you left for work, his car was parked outside his house?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You went to the brigade headquarters and at 6.00 you saw Mr. Cerkez there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, for how long were you and he together that morning?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went there for more than a couple of minutes, until the command came to the command post. I went to the MTS warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when did you next see Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when I saw him again during the day. I saw him a couple of times again, but I don't remember exactly at what time, because I was moving around between the warehouse to the headquarters and the headquarters of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. It's true that these places are close to one another, but I was moving from one to the other mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can try and think: Was it during the course of the morning that you saw Mr. Cerkez or may it have been in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the course of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, you have told us that you saw Mr. Cerkez that morning, the brigade commander, for only a couple of minutes. Could you tell the Chamber what you discussed that morning when you met.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember what we talked about. Probably he asked me what the situation was in the warehouse, whether we had people on duty, how we stood with the materiel. I believe that was what we must have spoken about, but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us make a more precise question. That morning, did Mr. Cerkez or any other person tell you anything in greater detail about the military situation, the current military operations that were going on?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one gave me any such information. I don't know whether such military information was conveyed to the other members of the command. Whether there was a briefing that morning, I wasn't present, so I was not informed about the situation. Whether the others were, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to return to this point of time, but I'm just going back a little bit earlier. In your evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to a slightly earlier period of time and then return to the night itself. In your evidence in chief you initially made no mention of, but later said you had remembered about the Kuber feature. Tell us, please, so that we've got the detail of your recollection in mind: How does the Kuber feature relate to what was to happen on the 15th, 16th of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at all how it affected it. I don't know what you're implying with that question. And I don't even know what was supposed to have happened on the 15th and 16th, except that it was stated that an attack by the BH army was expected on the 16th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what was the source of information what was expected, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of information regarding what was expected was the commander, Mario Cerkez, as he had come from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. In a brief briefing on the 15th, in the evening, as we said, it was said that a command had come from the Operative Zone to raise full combat readiness because there was a possibility of the BiH army attacking Vitez municipality from Kruscica and Vranjska. And the task of the brigade was to try and block those directions of attack from Kruscica and Vranjska towards Vitez. That was the source of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as I understand it -- let me just read your answer to myself again. You were expecting an attack at Kuber; is that the position? And you were taking action --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me again, then.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was stated that attack could occur, that they had some information that the attack could come from Kruscica and Vranjska towards the centre of town of Vitez. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Exactly. But there was no question of any attack having been already made on or by the 15th, was there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not right. In my examination-in-chief the other day, I said that in the brigade headquarters, the officer on duty had some information that on the 15th, in the afternoon or in the evening, a couple of trenches had fallen at the Kuber feature. I think it's Saracavica or something like that. But we were not informed of that until the next day whether it was true or not. Unfortunately, it was true. That detail at Kuber, the highest feature, had fallen, and we never restored control of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you, Major, that your differing answers in relation to Kuber, and indeed the very fact that you had to remember the evidence you were to give, shows that the answers you're giving about Kuber aren't true.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My testimony about Kuber and what I know about it is truthful, and I think that that is what I said the last time, because that is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when was Kuber attacked? On what day, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kuber was attacked already on the 15th, in the evening. A couple of trenches were captured. But a higher-intensity attack occurred on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that there was no preparation by the ABiH for any attack in the Lasva Valley by the sighting of ABiH soldiers in, for example, the school in Kruscica, your village? There were no such soldiers there, were there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have asked me two or three contradictory questions at the same time. I'll try and answer them as far as I am able. You said that I knew that the BH army was not trying to attack. That is not true. I don't know. I did not know their intentions. I knew nothing about them. I just said that there was information that an attack by the BiH army could occur. Then you also mentioned Kruscica. I know that I said -- I know that now, and I did see a BiH army unit in the elementary school in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, really? And when was that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the course of 1992, throughout, from the beginning of 1992 -- maybe I don't know exactly, but maybe from April or May, maybe earlier, and throughout. The strength was increasing all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'd like to look, please, at Exhibit 660 -- or 660.1, I think it is, technically. Major, you will have seen a lot of Blaskic orders in your time; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you therefore would know the style of a Blaskic order when you saw one; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at this document, looking at the original, and we have the English on the ELMO, please. Thank you very much. Don't be confused by the fact that there's no serial number at the top of the page above the date where there ought to be a serial number. That was apparently cut off by someone in a copying process and nothing to do with this case at all. So don't worry about that. But this document says that it's dated the 15th of April at 10.00 and it says, "According to reliable data, extremist Muslim forces continue their sabotage terrorist combat activities against members of the HVO and especially against the command cadre with the goal of frightening the military, liquidating the military commanders, bringing in confusion among the HVO ranks," and something about the military break-up of the HVO formations and ethnic cleansing of the territory. Does that seem to you to be Blaskic's normal style for writing military documents?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty but I think that Blaskic wrote this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please address the question. Is that style and the reference to things somewhat of generous and extreme terms, reference to ethnic cleansing and so on, is that his style or not?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next paragraph. "Until now, five violations of liquidations of commanders have been carried out, only one succeeded of the up-to-now five attempts at liquidation of the commander of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia." Can you point us to any other documents of the five attempts on the life of the commander of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia or the chief of the HVO, HZ HB which follows?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object. I don't think that there is any obligation on the witness to produce any kind of evidence in the meaning of documentary evidence. That's simply not his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can be asked if he knows anything about this allegation that there were five attempts on Colonel Blaskic's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but I am referring to the part of the section where the Prosecutor said, "Could you produce any evidence on that?" In the matter of fact of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can answer he can either say yes he's got a document or he can say no. Let's ask him this: Can you assist us, Major, with this allegation that there were five attempts on the life of the commander of the Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly about any such data. I know that there was an attempt in Zenica. The commander of that brigade, Zivko Totic, at that time and his he escort, three or four men were attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know about that.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also know about Novi Travnik, that two or three command members were intercepted a couple of days before and detained. I don't know about the rest. I don't remember. I have no information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who would the -- there's a reference to the chief of HVO, HZ HB. Who do you take that to be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna. The chief of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna. Probably the late Mate Boban. I think it was he. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, we read on in the same paragraph, "Probable intentions of further combat activity will be to occupy the structure, Kuber, and to cut off something from Vitez and to connect with their own forces across Poculica and Kuber." So one thing is quite clear, that if this document was written at 10.00 on the 15th of April, there was actually no evidence at that stage of any attack on Kuber; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that there's any evidence except for assumptions. I don't see that there is any evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next paragraph. "The auxiliary forces, they will exhibit activities in the directions already known with the goal of hiding their true intentions and connecting with parts of their forces. By unobjective informing, forces for psychological propaganda activity will create a space for justification of actions, because with their untruths, they will create the conviction that the Muslims are threatened on the territory under the HVO control."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say that this was translated in the Blaskic trial. I'm having it retranslated because it seems to me the language may not do justice to the document but I will press on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've read that last sentence, Major, in the original. Do you say that that sort of content is typical of Blaskic, reference to psychological propaganda as justification for actions?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, please may I be allowed to read it? I was listening to the Prosecutor and I couldn't read it at the same time. I was afraid of missing something so if I may read it to myself, please. I've read it through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say that's the style of Blaskic's normal communications, normal orders, or is there something different about this one?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I was no military expert, nor did I personally or directly receive any such orders. These were orders that were issued in the headquarters and started by the operative officers and they know these military terms. However, as far as I can tell, I think that what it says is true, and that these are assumptions regarding the intentions of the BiH army. I believe that the situation was as it is here described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last question on this part of the document, and only one other question on the document before I move on. Just below that, you'll see a reference to the night not of the 15th/16th but of the 14th/15th of April. If you'd like to read that to yourself, please, and we'll read it and then -- to save ourselves time -- and it can be seen on the ELMO. Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clearly, Major, I just suggest to you you have absolutely no recollection of reinforcements being brought to Kruscica on the night of the 14th/15th because if you had any such recollection, you would have told us about it already; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that nor did I know about it, but it need not mean that it did not happen because this order or this information I did not have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else, Major, from Kruscica, other than you, would be reporting such important events as the build up of troops in Kruscica along with Nadioci and Ahmici? Who, apart from you in Kruscica, would be making such a report?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us prepared such a report, I mean none of us from the Vitez Brigade and, in particular, from Kruscica. As far as I see, I was mistaken all the time. This document was drawn up in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia presumably on the basis of some intelligence information. This was not done by anyone from Kruscica or the brigade command. So it was not done in the Vitez Brigade, it was done in the Operative Zone on the basis of some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have told us last week that the assessment made was that the threat wasn't really a real one on this occasion. That's what you told us. I think if you look at the content of this last sentence, if there had been evidence of build-up of troops in Kruscica and Nadioci and Ahmici, nobody would have taken the view that it was other than a real threat; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree if such a document were shown, then I would have thought it was a genuine threat, but I didn't know about this document. I didn't know about the information in this document. I suppose that other members of the command neither saw it nor knew it. But as we talked among ourselves and we did not think that there would be any serious escalation of the conflict, then perhaps some minor incidents could happen, but that nothing serious would happen, basically. So that we did not really have this in mind, and that is why several members of our command, we simply did not think that something serious would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your briefing by Cerkez, nothing was said about the areas of Nadioci or Ahmici or Pirici or Sivrino because, of course, if anything had been said about them you'd have been deployed there to defend the areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not informed about anything at the briefing with Mario Cerkez or about Ahmici, Nadioci, Sivrino Selo or anything else except Kruscica and Vranjska. That was the only thing that we were informed about. If I need to repeat, I have already repeated it several times today, what we have been told at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we turn to the next page, the bottom of the page as far as you are concerned, and the next page on the English, under 2.1, the battalion of the military police where we see an emphasis on the fact that the commander of the 4th Battalion is directly responsible for the security of the forward command post in Vitez. Then we see later on this, and perhaps you would follow this in the original while I read the English, "In the event of a rather strong attack by the Muslim extremist forces from the direction of the villages Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino, Pirici, inform me." There was nothing said to you that night at all to suggest that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was a probability or a possibility of attack by Muslim extremist forces in those villages, was there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: True. We were told nothing that night about these directions of attack or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now see a different exhibit. It's a new exhibit, it's 653.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, the brigade of the 1st Battalion of the Vitez -- let's have a look at this document, you must help me with it. This is a document dated the 14th of April headed the Viteska Brigade, and it lists personnel from the 1st Battalion. Tell us about the 1st Battalion, please. What was the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade was the battalion which had some 300 men. That was its roster, and those soldiers from the 1st Battalion went -- were summoned to the front lines against the army of Republika Srpska and the JNA. That is in Jajce, up there in Vlasic, Turbe, above Novi Travnik, Slatka voda, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The first battalion, you say of 300, was, as it were, the active battalion to be distinguished from what had been called here "village guards"; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion was an active duty only depending on how many men had been called up to do a shift, so there would be active duty for those eight to ten days while they were on a shift, and after that, they were free men, free citizens; that is, come back from the shift and go back to their homes, back to their regular jobs, chores and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see here it's broken down by company. 1st Company, 2nd Company, 3rd Company, and then as to the 1st Company with its commander, Slavko Papic, it makes it plain that there were 20 soldiers in Nadioci and 12 in Santici. And that's where those men were positioned at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not true. Those soldiers -- 20 Nadioci; Santici, 12 of them -- these are soldiers who are members of the battalion of the Viteska Brigade. And when was this written? Where were they at that time, I don't know. This document simply says what was the numerical strength in the battalion of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The title of the document is the list of personnel, their number, from the 1st Battalion, positioned in the villages.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can see that the 1st Company covers a series of villages entirely different from the villages covered by the 2nd Company, which I think is entirely different from the villages covered by the 3rd Company. So this is the disposition, the positioning of soldiers, and 20 of them were in Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from the transcript. I will not interrupt the answer.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true what you say, that those soldiers were in Nadioci at that time, Santici, Dubravica, and so on and so forth. This list shows how many men from those villages were members of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade. That is how many men they had on their list. And the battalion had about 300. But it's not true that they were in those villages at that time. They are simply residents of those villages. That's where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is now clear, but that was just a part which was missing on line 14 at page 28. Now it is out of my screen, so I cannot see it. There the witness just mentioned, and that was not in the transcript, "from the villages." That was missing. But I think after this it is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, can you -- you may be right. Who knows? It's not the interpretation I'm going to argue for this document at this stage. But can you point me, so that I can check your answer, to a document that will show me that the 1st Company was chosen from exclusively Nadioci, Santici, Dubravica, Poculica and Rijeka? The figure for Rijeka I think must be 28. Can you point us to a document that shows that that's how those companies were composed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot show the document which I don't have. I'm only saying those things which I know and which sound logical to me. A battalion has three companies, and from what I can gather from this document -- and this is the first time I see it in my life. I never saw it before -- I see that it is somehow divided territorially, from Nadioci to Rijeka, the first part, where we have the 1st Company of the battalion; whereas the 2nd Company is between Mosunj and Bila. They are all neighbouring villages. And the third one again, Zaselje, Veceriska, Krcevine, Stari Vitez, and so on. I do not have any documents, and this is the first time that I see this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or is the truth, Major, that Viteska Brigade soldiers were indeed positioned in Nadioci and Santici a day before those villages and Ahmici were the subject of attack?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the night of the 15th, because I want to ask you a few more questions about that. You're telling us, I think, or you told us last week, that you went in at the broken-off wedding celebrations -- or that Cerkez went in, I beg your pardon, at about what, 4.00, was it, 4.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 4.00 in the afternoon is when we returned home that 15th of April, planning to have a bath and get ready for the wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you went back when Cerkez went back? Did you go back with him? I've forgotten. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Excuse me. I'm too fast. I did not come back with Cerkez, because I stayed home, took my shower, shaved, and was getting ready to go. I was waiting for him to go to his wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It comes to this: After you were called back for your briefing, Cerkez then went away, I think you told us, for a long time, apparently to Blaskic's headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a short briefing, in the evening of the 15th, Cerkez went somewhere, and I do not know exactly where. All that I would say would be an assumption. I do not really know exactly where he went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he came back, when you met again, where were the two of you? In your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he returned the next morning -- and I said the next morning around 6.00, but I'm not sure, because I did not look at the watch -- it was at the headquarters of the brigade, at the Workers' University, which housed the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's my mistake and I'm sorry. He went away. Did you then go home that same evening, the 15th, and simply spend the evening at home?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left too around midnight. I went home and spent the night at home, until 5.00 in the morning of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you first saw Cerkez on the morning of the 16th, what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said nothing to me personally. I don't remember what he said. There was gunfire. Most of the members of the command were there. I can't remember what we were saying, even what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Think back, Major. Didn't you want to know what had happened?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We wanted to know what had happened. But we saw what had happened. Vitez had been shelled. There was gunfire from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't interested in knowing what briefing Cerkez had had the night before, when his planned wedding had to be aborted?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I been alone with him, had there been nobody else, perhaps we might have talked about it. But after that, in the morning, when the gunfire started, what I was interested to know was to see my situation, to see how I could get around and get something, because I knew that we had very little materiel in our storage space, in our depot, and that was my principal concern. That is what I was obsessed by throughout the war, not only during those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you at any time, Major, asked Cerkez what happened at that late-night briefing or that evening briefing? Have you at no time asked him what happened?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not ask him, at no time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He never told you one word about it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not say a word to me, because as far as I can remember, I never had the opportunity to talk to him. Had we been alone, one on one, perhaps I would have asked him, but it simply did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're suggesting, on the evidence that you have, that he was away -- I beg your pardon -- he was back home that night, simply because his car was outside the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is why I thought that he was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us -- I'm not in any position to accept or to challenge it -- that Cerkez had in the past been engaged on active missions, leading people into battle, as it were; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a couple of occasions, perhaps four or five times in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, from everything you've heard, that on the night of the 15th, 16th, the Viteska Brigade was involved in something; and the military police and the Jokers, and it may be the Vitezovi and other units, were also engaged in activity immediately around Vitez. You know that, don't you, from all you've heard?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that, because the Viteska Brigade was not engaged anywhere between the 15th and the 16th except Novi Travnik, that is, the defence line above Novi Travnik against the ARS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Perhaps I'll have a look at another map with you about that. But my question to you is this: If this Chamber in due course decides that there was a concerted action that night involving a number of military units, if that's what this Chamber decides -- follow me -- can you think of any reason why Cerkez would not be leading his men?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a joint action, as far as I know. And Cerkez led his command. He's the one who leads it. So he naturally leads and commands his subordinate officers in the chain of the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. So if there was an action on that night, the 15th, 16th, involving the Viteska Brigade, Cerkez would not have been at home; he would have been leading his men. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had the brigade been engaged anywhere, in the 15th in the evening and the morning of the 16th, Cerkez would not be leading his men like Sava Kovacevic, with a rifle in his hand, but it would have been the leader of the company. But that night nothing happened here. There was only men, commander of the shift, which was in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, for some reason, like Sajevic having a cold, Cerkez was unable to lead his men, who would be the man in charge? Again, just help me with that as a hypothesis, because that's what we have to deal with. Assume that there was an action that night. Assume that for some reason Cerkez can't lead his men. Who would be in charge, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've lost the translation. Are we getting the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we try again? Can you repeat your answer, please. The question was who would be in charge if Mr. Cerkez wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you asked, Your Honour, last time, there was a mistake in the translation. There was no conditional. It was like "who was," not "who would be."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not getting any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's why he reacted differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Croatian translation which we did get at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may have got it, but we have nothing. Well, it's about time for a break. Perhaps somebody would look into the problem over the adjournment. We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, assuming we now have the English translation which we didn't before the break, no fault of yours, of course, if Cerkez wasn't in charge of an operation on that night, who would have been leading his men?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that that night there was any kind of operation by the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm just saying if there was, who would be in charge if Cerkez was at home in bed?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the assumption that anything had happened, that there was any activity, if we were to assume that, I think that if he were not there, if the commander were not there, then the unit would be commanded by the chief of staff or perhaps somebody else who would be authorised by the commander, perhaps the commander of a battalion. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. New topic or at least a different topic. If the forces of the Viteska Brigade were obliged to occupy defensive positions and to blockade several positions in the Vitez area, the operation would require your involvement; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something like that was supposed to be done, my participation would probably have been involved in the sense of logistic support to a unit that was supposed to carry out a particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'd obviously have to know about the plan and you would find yourself giving logistical support to one or the other of the involved groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the way it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the brigade headquarters at 6.00 on the morning of the 16th having left, as I checked from your evidence last week, at about midnight the night before, when you arrived at 6.00 in the morning, there was no suggestion, no evidence, no indication that the Viteska Brigade had been engaged in any activity the previous night; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to headquarters at 5.00 in the morning and there was no indication that the Viteska Brigade --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry I seem to have lost the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The translation is okay but that's where the witness stopped, you interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No indication that the Viteska Brigade what?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it had operated anywhere that night between the 15th and 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said something about Novi Travnik and the involvement of the group at Novi Travnik. What were you telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that from November 1992, Vitez -- well, first the municipal staff sent a unit consisting of perhaps two platoons to the defence line above Novi Travnik facing the army of Republika Srpska and the JNA. Slatka voda, Kamenjas, Mravinac, Vucja Glava, that area. And they were sent until the conflict with the BH army started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having arrived at 5.00 in the morning and Cerkez coming in at 6.00, how were the troops thereafter disposed, please, and whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having come in at 6.00, I don't know that the forces, the troops went anywhere except that they were perhaps in the area of Vranjska and Kruscica. I don't know that exactly, and we also had a unit consisting of 50 men in Novi Travnik up there. They were there for another day or two until they managed to get out. We did not have any troops of the Viteska Brigade anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would be good enough please to look at this exhibit which is our D85/2 on the computer. Now, if you look at that map, you haven't seen it before, take your time, what do you say of the suggestion that the green lines might reflect, very broadly, the division of Croat areas from Muslim areas. Are they about right or are they definitely wrong or what do you say? I don't want to hurry you but just in general terms, but don't worry too much about the detail. It's just in general terms because it's a roughish map, do the green lines look to you to be about right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major, if you don't follow the map, just say so.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately it is accurate. I'm not very good at maps at all because I'm not a military expert. I don't -- I can't see this very well, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's focus, if the booth would be good enough, on the blue line, get in as close as we can, and enlarge it. That's very helpful, thank you. Now, just look at the blue line, Major, please. Were anyone to suggest that on either the night of the 15th, the night of the 16th or the day of the 17th, were anyone to suggest that the Viteska Brigade was deployed along those blue lines, such evidence would be wholly wrong, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain then, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here that the blue line, as you say, the forces of the brigade, goes from Safradinovo Selo, Rijeka. Yes, all right. And then up here, up here, I can't read this. As for these two middle lines, I think that's all right. But Safradinovo Selo, I don't think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But all right as depicting what and when?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand this. Could you repeat it more specifically?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll go back to my previous question because I think it's easier. That blue line does not depict, does it, on your recollection of events, depict deployment of the Viteska Brigade on the night of the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not depict the deployment of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does not depict the deployment of the Viteska Brigade on the 16th, either.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not depict it on the 16th either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th, I can't remember exactly. That is when mobilisation had already occurred, and people from the villages stood on the borders of their villages and from that day, from the 16th of the afternoon and the 17th, people were already mobilised. And once they were mobilised, they were under the command of the Viteska Brigade. Possibly that is what the situation could have been from the 17th onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I want you to see another document, please, which we'll lay over the map, and it's Exhibit 676. I'm afraid this document has been given other numbers, but if we operate on 676. Perhaps you'd like to look at this document, please, Major. Again, don't, for the time being, be distracted by the fact that someone has deleted the serial number from the top of the document. That's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nothing to do with anything in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And incidentally, I can tell the Court that I am now in a position to provide, in due course, a full original for the earlier document with the missing serial number, which we'll probably have to look at in some detail, the one on the 15th, and I hope to be able to do the same with this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document purports to be a command given at 1.30 on the morning of the 16th of April. On your evidence, Major, no such order was given and received by Cerkez that night, was it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what the order says. It says: "On the basis of command and assessment made, we expect an enemy attack," and it sets out some further details. And then under item 2 it says the assignment of your forces is to occupy the defence region, blockade the villages, and prevent entrances to and exits from the villages. It says that the time of readiness for the attack is 0530 hours on the 16th. And it then sets out, at number 3, where Cerkez was to find the 4th Battalion of the Military Police and the Zrinjski Brigade, and so on. Now, on your evidence, no such order can have been given, can it?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of this order, and I don't know. I doubt that the commander got it. He never showed it to us. I had never seen this order, except that he told us orally that in the evening of the 15th of April, that an order was supposed to come in, combat readiness was supposed to be raised, because a possible attack by the BH army is expected from the directions that I mentioned: Kruscica, Vranjska, et cetera. I was not aware of all the rest. I'm not aware of all the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I can probably close this part of my cross-examination with this suggestion or question to you: If this order, which you can now see for the first time before you, had resulted in -- have another look at it, please -- the disposition of troops shown on the blue line on the map by 5.30 on the morning of the 16th, you would have known about that on the morning of the 16th for sure, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably would have known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us at all to unlock a problem that we face? Can you help us at all with why the man Zeljko Sajevic, who you spoke of as a person who, but for his cold, would have had good knowledge of events, should have drawn the map that you're looking at as representing the disposition of troops at half past 5.00 on the morning of the 16th? Can you help us at all with why he might have done that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Zeljko drew this and deployed it this way. I don't know. But I know that Zeljko is an operations man and that he's very good at maps. In our command, he -- well, he was not a professional soldier, but he was one of those who was the most familiar with military terminology, and I think that he had spent all his career working at the Territorial Defence headquarters and places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Prosecution side to give different explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, you'll have to start again. The interpretation was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be better if I spoke in Croatian. I think that it is not all right if the Prosecutor interprets the answer of the previous witness and then puts it to this witness. The previous witness, when shown this picture, he said what the deployment should have been. In this way, the witness is being confronted with a claim that was not made in an improper way, and I think that this should be rejected all together. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's absolutely not my understanding of the previous witness's evidence. And indeed, had it not been the purpose of the evidence to lead the Chamber to believe that those were where the troops were on the night in question, the evidence simply would not have been led at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We now have the evidence. Perhaps you would check, because I don't have my notes with me, as to what the Major said about those blue lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think this witness can assist any further on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I agree entirely, and I'm going to conclude the Ahmici questions with just a few more and then I'm going to try and cover most of what else I want to cover by hacking back on the topics to be covered by lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the last witness said -- just to answer Your Honour's question, he tried to depict on the map the positions of the personnel of the Viteska Brigade on the 16th of April at half past 5.00. And then at a later stage, in answer indeed to Your Honour, I think, seeking to clarify matters, he said: [As read] "This is what I wanted to show. It was the situation, the deployment at half past 5.00 in the morning based on the order received. That is where our forces were to be at that time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not dispute this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will not, Your Honour, but just one point so we have a clear situation. It is now explained. But the same situation, I will remind the Court, was in Elford presentation, and also the same criteria. What should have been according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if the order had been followed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I just may add: We will bring the witnesses who will explain what actually was on the field. What I'm trying to say: There is no need to investigate now on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel is entitled, provided he does it accurately, to put matters to the witness to test the witness's recollection and to get his response.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I? May I go back to this a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've finished this line. If Mr. Kovacic wants to ask you any more questions about it, he can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, on that night, on the night of the 15th of April, there was a meeting, and at that meeting it was perfectly clear -- and if you were there, you know this -- that the Viteska Brigade were going to be involved with the Jokers, the military police, and others in a joint operation?

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have put a question that's a bit complicated. On the 15th, in the evening, the only thing I know -- or rather the members of the command of the Viteska Brigade was that an order would arrive from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, raising combat readiness, because there were indications that the forces of the BH army could attack Vitez from the direction of Kruscica and Vranjska, with the intention of entering Vitez, the town of Vitez. That is what we know that evening. We don't know anything else. Now you are referring to some other units, some other assignments. I don't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ceko. In the question put to you by Mr. Nice, it was quite clear. He is asking you to give a clear answer, that is, by saying "yes" or "no": Did you that evening discuss a joint operation of the Viteska Brigade, to which you belonged, and a joint operation together with other units, such as the military police or the Jokers? That is the question. Did you that evening discuss a joint operation? So the answer should be "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: STIPO CEKO [Resumed]
